Vesuvius Challenge · First Letters

Scroll Scout

Before anyone spends GPU time on a Herculaneum scroll, Scroll Scout predicts whether a seed point will give a clean papyrus surface, from a few megabytes of public CT data, on a laptop CPU. It is tested against 65 patches judged by eye and maps all 21 scrolls still eligible for the $50,000 First Letters prizes.

0.88held-out AUC on scrolls the score never saw
2.8×more good seeds in its top 10 than random placement (50% vs 18%)
21unread scrolls mapped, 1344 points scored
0GPUs needed: everything streams from the open-data bucket

The problem

Every attempt to read an unread scroll starts by growing a surface on one papyrus sheet inside the CT scan, then running an ink model on it. In crushed parts of a scroll the sheets touch and fuse, the grown surface jumps between them, and the ink model sees noise. In the First Letters survey, only 12 of 65 automatically grown patches on the eligible scrolls stayed on their sheet over most of their area. Ink inference on the rest is wasted.

What the scout sees

Around a point, Scroll Scout reads a 3.3 mm cube of the CT and of the published surface-m7 prediction at pyramid level 1 (17 µm voxels) and measures five things: are the predicted sheets flat, unfused and unfragmented, and does the sheet orientation, in the prediction and in the raw CT, avoid swirling?

Does it work?

Ground truth is the survey's verdict for each of its 65 patches: did the grown surface stay on the sheet? 12 did. The score was tested two ways.

scoreAUC95% CItop-10 precision
no ranking (the survey’s grid of seeds)0.50–18%
v1, terms fixed before looking at results0.84 0.73–0.9350%
v2, leave-one-scroll-out0.88 0.78–0.9550%

Leave-one-scroll-out means: for each of the 21 scrolls, the signals were chosen using the other 20 only, then tested on the held-out scroll. The same four signals were chosen in all 21 rounds. Both results have a permutation p-value of 0.0002.

Where text was actually found

Two scrolls on the same 8.64 µm, 116 keV scan protocol as most eligible scrolls have produced text: PHerc. 343, whose 18 letters won the October First Letters prize, and PHerc. 1447, where the team found text in September. The scout scored those exact places against random points inside the same scrolls.

The atlas

64 points were spread through each of the 21 eligible scroll volumes (8 heights × 4 distances from the axis) and scored. Scrolls are ranked by their best 10% of points. The seed shown is each scroll's best point in its inner part (within 0.45 of the way from the axis to the outside, away from the top and bottom 15%), where both known text finds lie, as level-0 voxel coordinates (x y z) of the eligible volume. Copy puts a ready-to-run fls.py command on the clipboard. More seeds per scroll, inner and overall, are in atlas/seeds.csv.

Use it

pip install "git+https://github.com/tkran2/scrollscout"
scrollscout point PHerc0268 20251110183117 7936 6608 5936     # score one point (x y z)
scrollscout scan  PHerc0268 20251110183117 --points 64         # map one scroll, pick seeds
scrollscout atlas --out atlas/                                 # every First Letters volume

No GPU, no VC3D install and no full-volume downloads: the tool reads only the chunks it needs from s3://vesuvius-challenge-open-data. Source, tests and every script behind these numbers: https://github.com/tkran2/scrollscout.

Limits

The ground truth is one survey: 65 patches, one tracer (GrowPatch), judged by one person. A clean surface is necessary for reading text, not sufficient: the scout says where tracing works, not where the ink is. The atlas samples 64 points per scroll, so its seeds are the best of those points, not the best in the scroll.

CT scans and surface predictions: Vesuvius Challenge open data (CC BY-NC 4.0); figures derived from them carry the same licence. Ground truth: First Letters survey by Matteo Bulloni. PHerc. 343 letter locations: Erwin Nieuwlaar's winning submission. Code: MIT.
